title: Spotting constellations
keyIdea: A constellation is a pattern of stars. The Plough is 7 bright stars shaped like a pan with a bent handle. The 2 stars at the end of the pan are the pointers: follow them about 5 gaps to the North Star. The North Star is only medium bright, but it stays nearly still while the whole sky turns round it in the night.
familyTip: On a clear night, face north and look for the Plough. In the UK you can see it on any clear night of the year. Ask your child to find the pointers and hop to the North Star. Look again an hour later and see how far the Plough has turned. Use a star map app only to check, not to find.

visual.caption: True about stars, or a mix-up? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The North Star stays nearly still
The North Star is the brightest star
Stars are still there in the day
Stars go away in the day
The Plough can flip like a mirror

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the Plough, follow the pointers to the North Star, watch the night turn, check a robot's star facts.

kid: Stars make patterns in the sky. A star pattern with a name is a constellation. The Plough is easy to spot. It has 7 bright stars. 4 make a pan and 3 make a bent handle.
Find the 2 stars at the end of the pan, away from the handle. They are the pointers. Go up from them about 5 times the gap. You reach the North Star.
The North Star is not the brightest star. Lots of stars shine more. But it stays nearly still. In the night the other stars turn round it, so the Plough can look upside down.
Stars do not go away in the day. They are still there. The Sun is so bright that we cannot see them.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. The US science standard 1-ESS1-1 asks young children to describe patterns of the Sun, Moon and stars that can be predicted. Key words: star, constellation, star pattern, the Plough (the Big Dipper in the US), pointer stars, the North Star (Polaris). The Plough is strictly part of a bigger constellation, the Great Bear (Ursa Major).

The most common mistake is thinking the North Star is the brightest star. It is only medium bright, about the 48th brightest; Sirius is the brightest star at night. The North Star matters because it sits almost above Earth's North Pole, so it stays nearly still and shows which way is north.

Other common mix-ups: stars vanish in the day (sunlight hides them), the Plough stays still (it turns round the North Star once a day because Earth spins), and an upside-down Plough is a new pattern. The sky turns patterns round but never flips them like a mirror.

In the lab your child finds the 7 Plough stars among many, taps the pointers and follows a line of 5 gaps to the North Star, moves the night on 6 hours and sees the Plough turn while the North Star stays put, picks the Plough from flipped and other patterns, and checks a robot's star facts.

practice.prompt: A cloud hides {a} stars of the Plough. How many of its 7 stars can you still see?
practice.hint: The Plough has 7 stars. Take away the ones behind the cloud.
practice.explain: 7 take away {a} is {=7-a}. The Plough always has 7 bright stars, even when some are hidden.

practice.prompt: You have found {a} stars of the Plough. How many more do you need to find?
practice.hint: There are 4 stars in the pan and 3 in the handle. That is 7.
practice.explain: The Plough has 7 stars, so you need {=7-a} more.

practice.prompt: Which stars point to the North Star?
choices: The 2 at the end of the pan
practice.hint: Find the side of the pan that is far from the handle.
practice.explain: The 2 stars at the end of the pan, away from the handle, are the pointers. Follow them about 5 gaps.

practice.prompt: Is the North Star the brightest star?
choices: It is a planet, not a star
practice.hint: Do you find the North Star by its brightness or by the pointers?
practice.explain: The North Star is only medium bright. Sirius is the brightest star at night. You find the North Star with the pointers.

practice.prompt: Where are the stars in the daytime?
practice.hint: The stars do not move away. What is very bright in the day?
practice.explain: The stars are still in the sky in the day. The Sun is so bright that we cannot see them.

pool.prompt: The pointers are {a} fingers apart when you hold your hand out. The North Star is about 5 times as far. How many fingers is that?
pool.hint: Count the gap 5 times, or use your 5 times table.
pool.explain: 5 gaps of {a} fingers is {=5*a} fingers up from the pointers.

pool.prompt: The W of Cassiopeia has 5 stars. You can see {a} of them. How many are hidden?
pool.hint: The W has 5 stars. Take away the ones you can see.

pool.prompt: How many bright stars make the Plough?
pool.hint: Count the pan and the handle.
pool.explain: 4 stars in the pan and 3 in the handle make 7. The W of Cassiopeia has 5.

pool.prompt: You watch all night. Which star stays nearly still?
pool.hint: The whole sky turns round one star.
pool.explain: The North Star stays nearly still. The Plough and the other stars turn round it.

pool.prompt: The Plough looks upside down. Why?
pool.hint: Are they the same 7 stars in the same shape?
pool.explain: The same 7 stars keep their shape. The sky has turned, so the Plough is a different way up.

choices: A pattern of stars with a name
pool.hint: Think of the Plough: lots of stars making one shape.
pool.explain: A constellation is a named pattern of stars, like the Great Bear that holds the Plough.

pool.prompt: Which way is the North Star?
pool.hint: Its name tells you which way to face to find it.
pool.explain: The North Star is in the north. In the UK it is high in the sky, but not right above you.

pool.prompt: Which picture can never be the Plough?
choices: The Plough flipped like in a mirror
pool.hint: The sky turns the pattern round. Does it ever flip it?
pool.explain: The sky turns the Plough round, so it can be on its side or upside down. It never flips like a mirror.
